evidence: Caes. B.G. 6.29.3: in longitūdinem pedum ducentōrum
Cic. N.D. 1.54: lātitūdinum, longitūdinum, altitūdinum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In length, lengthwise: in longitūdinem (Caes., Cic.). A length is usually given with the adjective and an accusative of measure, curriculum longum sescentōs pedēs, a course six hundred feet long (Gell. 1.1.2, Lewis & Short s.v. sescentī), or with longitūdō and a genitive, as Caesar does. Of time it is rarer (longitūdō noctis, Cic.); for a long time see long time.

phrases.english: he cut down the far end of the bridge for a length of two hundred feet

phrases.english: for each foot of length, one measure of lime and two of sand

phrases.english: trusting the length of her neck to his throat, she performed a dangerous cure on the wolf
